expectations.text: The skill discovers and reads the existing rules file before writing anything
expectations.evidence: The transcript states 'Read the existing file. The file already has a Debugging section with a guideline about using a logger utility instead of raw console.* calls.' The output preserves all original content (Code Style, Debugging, Testing sections), confirming the file was read before modification.

expectations.text: It asks which section the rule belongs in (or suggests Code Style)
expectations.evidence: No evidence in the transcript of asking the user or suggesting a section. The agent unilaterally chose the Debugging section without any interactive confirmation step.

expectations.text: The rule text is one clear imperative sentence, not a paragraph or multi-sentence explanation
expectations.evidence: The rule text is a bold header ('No console.log in committed code.') followed by three additional sentences explaining scope, acceptable use, and alternatives. This is a multi-sentence paragraph, not a single imperative sentence.

expectations.text: The rule is classified as T1 (console.log has a clear syntactic signature)
expectations.evidence: No tier classification (T1, T2, T3, etc.) appears anywhere in the transcript or the output file. The enforcement block exists but lacks any tier label.

expectations.text: The enforcement block has a regex pattern matching console.log
expectations.evidence: The enforcement block contains: check: grep -rn "console\.\(log\|debug\|info\|warn\)" --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx" src/ — This grep BRE pattern matches console.log (and related methods).

expectations.text: The rule is appended to an appropriate section, not dumped at the end of the file
expectations.evidence: The rule was added as a bullet under the existing 'Debugging' section (line 15), and the enforcement block appears between Debugging and Testing sections. The file structure is preserved.

expectations.text: Budget checks run after generating the block
expectations.evidence: No mention of budget checks, token counts, line counts, or any size validation in the transcript or outputs.

claims.claim: The file already has a Debugging section with a guideline about using a logger utility
claims.evidence: The output file line 14 shows the pre-existing bullet: 'If persistent logging is genuinely needed (e.g., error reporting), use a dedicated logger utility instead of raw console.* calls.'

claims.claim: console.error is intentionally excluded because it often serves a legitimate runtime purpose
claims.evidence: The grep pattern 'console.\(log\|debug\|info\|warn\)' excludes console.error. The reasoning is stated in transcript step 2.

claims.claim: The enforcement block was placed immediately after the Debugging section, before Testing
claims.evidence: In the output, the ENFORCEMENT comment block (lines 17-21) appears between the Debugging content and the '## Testing' heading (line 24).

suggestions.assertion: The skill discovers and reads the existing rules file before writing anything
suggestions.reason: The transcript is a self-authored summary, not a tool-call log. Any agent could claim it read the file. A stronger eval would capture actual tool calls (Read before Write) or check that original content is preserved verbatim — the latter is partially what I used but is indirect.

suggestions.assertion: The enforcement block has a regex pattern matching console.log
suggestions.reason: This passes for any pattern that matches console.log, but doesn't check whether the pattern is well-formed or avoids false positives (e.g., matching 'console.logger' or strings in comments). Consider testing the pattern against sample inputs.

No assertion checks whether the enforcement block follows a consistent schema (trigger/check/expect/message fields). The agent invented its own format. A skill-driven run should produce a standardized format; an assertion verifying schema conformance would discriminate between skill and no-skill runs.

eval_feedback.overall: The without-skill run produced a reasonable result but missed several structured-workflow expectations (tier classification, budget checks, user confirmation of section). The assertions are well-targeted at differentiating skill-guided behavior from ad-hoc generation.
